hero.title: Mercedes-Benz M113 Engine - Replacement Cost, Problems & Compatibility
hero.description: The M113 is Mercedes-Benz’s legendary 4.3-litre to 5.5-litre V8 petrol engine, famous for its bulletproof reliability, 3-valve-per-cylinder design, and the introduction of the high-performance "Kompressor" (supercharged) AMG variants. Fitted to the W210/W211 E-Class, W220 S-Class, W463 G-Class, and various AMG models, reconditioned M113 engines typically start from £2,000 , serving as a highly sought-after, robust unit for classic Mercedes restorations and performance builds.

costGuide.title: Mercedes-Benz M113 Engine Replacement Cost (UK)
costGuide.labourLine: Fitting an M113 engine typically takes 10-14 hours at £65-£85/hr (independent) - confirm exact labour when comparing quotes.
paragraphs: What genuinely moves the price for this engine is the condition of the valley cover gasket, crankshaft position sensor (CPS), and (on AMG Kompressor models) the supercharger coupler and snout bearings. Because the M113 is a robust but aging V8, recon specialists will typically replace the valley cover gasket, fit a new CPS, and refurbish or replace the Kompressor unit as standard to prevent immediate post-installation failures. For a full breakdown of market rates, see our full reconditioned engine cost guide.

failures.title: Mercedes-Benz M113 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Crankshaft Position Sensor (CPS) Failure - All variants
items.whatHappens: The CPS is located at the rear of the engine block, near the firewall, where it is exposed to extreme heat cycles. The internal wiring degrades, causing the sensor to fail when the engine is hot. This results in sudden stalling, a no-start condition, or rough running until the engine cools down.
items.repairVsReplace: Replacing the CPS is a relatively inexpensive and straightforward repair, though access is tight. It is highly recommended to replace the sensor proactively during any major engine service.

items.title: Valley Cover Gasket Leak - All variants
items.whatHappens: The plastic valley cover gasket (located between the two cylinder heads) hardens and shrinks over time, allowing oil to leak directly into the spark plug wells. This causes misfires, rough idling, and can eventually lead to ignition coil failure or burning oil smells from the exhaust.
items.repairVsReplace: This is a routine maintenance item. Replacing the valley cover gasket and spark plug tube seals is relatively inexpensive in terms of parts, though it requires removing the intake manifold for proper access.

items.title: Balance Shaft Gear Wear - Early variants
items.whatHappens: The balance shafts, designed to smooth out V8 vibrations, are driven by small gears that can wear or shear over time, particularly on early production models. This triggers crankshaft position sensor error codes, causes a rough idle, and in severe cases, broken gear fragments can jam the oil pump or timing chain.
items.repairVsReplace: If caught early, replacing the balance shaft assembly and gears is a known, albeit labour-intensive, repair. If the oil pump or timing has been compromised, a full reconditioned M113 unit is required.

items.title: Kompressor Coupler and Snout Wear - Supercharged AMG variants (.970, .980)
items.whatHappens: The Eaton M112 supercharger uses a plastic/rubber coupler to connect the drive pulley to the internal rotors. Over time, this coupler disintegrates, resulting in a loud rattling or whining noise from the front of the engine and a complete loss of boost pressure.
items.repairVsReplace: The coupler can be replaced independently as a relatively inexpensive maintenance item. However, if the snout bearings have failed and scored the housing, a full supercharger rebuild or replacement is necessary.

failures.goodYearsLine: The M113 is widely regarded as one of the most durable and reliable V8 engines Mercedes ever produced. Post-2000 units with revised balance shaft gear materials and updated CPS wiring show significantly improved longevity, routinely exceeding 250,000 miles without major internal bottom-end issues .

variants.title: M113 Sub-Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Car?
variants.intro: ═══════════════════════════════════════ INTRO: The M113 family shares the same fundamental SOHC 24-valve V8 block architecture, but displacement and the presence of the Eaton supercharger (on AMG variants) vary significantly. Identifying your exact sub-code is mandatory, as fitting the wrong revision can lead to severe mechanical and ECU incompatibility. - Fitted to: C-Class W202 (C 43 AMG), E-Class W210 (E 430), S-Class W220 (S 430), G-Class W463 (G 430), M-Class W163 (ML 430) - Key technical difference: The entry-level V8 variant, designed to offer a smooth, torque-rich upgrade over the inline-6 models, featuring port fuel injection and a focus on reliable daily driving. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; no unique widespread defects beyond standard CPS and valley cover gasket wear. - Interchange note: Not a straight swap with larger displacement variants due to different engine mounts, wiring harnesses, and ECU mapping. - Fitted to: E-Class W210 (E 500), S-Class W220 (S 500), SL-Class R230 (SL 500) - Key technical difference: The volume-seller 5.0L variant, featuring a longer stroke for higher low-end torque, making it the preferred choice for the heavier W220 S-Class and grand touring SL chassis. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; early models are particularly susceptible to balance shaft gear wear. - Interchange note: Requires matching sump and accessory drives; passenger car variants are not directly interchangeable with commercial/off-road specs without modification. - Fitted to: E-Class W210 (E 55 AMG), S-Class W220 (S 55 AMG), M-Class W163 (ML 55 AMG) - Key technical difference: The naturally aspirated AMG variant, featuring a stroked 5.5L displacement, revised cylinder head casting, aggressive camshaft profiles, and upgraded cooling to handle high-performance demands. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; the higher continuous thermal loads can accelerate valve cover and oil seal degradation. - Interchange note: Not interchangeable with standard 5.0L variants without swapping the intake manifold, exhaust, and specific AMG ECU mapping. - Fitted to: S-Class W220 (S 55 AMG Kompressor), CL-Class C215 (CL 55 AMG Kompressor) - Key technical difference: The legendary supercharged flagship variant, featuring an Eaton M112 supercharger, forged internals, upgraded cooling, and aggressive engine management to deliver effortless, massive torque. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; supercharger coupler degradation and intercooler pump failures are the primary unique wear items. - Interchange note: Not interchangeable with naturally aspirated variants without swapping the supercharger, intake manifold, exhaust, and specific AMG ECU mapping. - Fitted to: CLK-Class W209 (CLK 55 AMG Kompressor), SL-Class R230 (SL 55 AMG) - Key technical difference: The highest-output M113 variant, featuring a revised supercharger pulley, updated intercooler system, and specific calibration for the lighter CLK and SL chassis, delivering sports-car performance. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; the higher boost pressures place additional stress on the supercharger snout bearings and coupler. - Interchange note: Shares the core supercharged architecture with the .980, but the engine mounts, wiring harness routing, and ECU mapping are specific to the W209/R230 chassis.

relatives.description: the older 4.2L-5.0L V8 that the M113 replaced, sharing the same robust V8 philosophy but transitioning to a simpler, more reliable SOHC 3-valve architecture.

the modern 4.6L-5.5L V8 that eventually replaced the M113 across the E-Class, S-Class, and G-Class range, introducing 4-valve-per-cylinder technology, variable valve timing, and improved emissions compliance.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement M113 Engine - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used M113 engine makes sense only if it comes with verifiable service history and documented proof of a recent valley cover gasket replacement, CPS replacement, and (for AMG models) supercharger coupler inspection. Given the risk of balance shaft failure on early models, buying a used unit with unknown history is a significant financial risk.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper reconditioned M113 engine is the sweet spot for most buyers. A reputable rebuild will proactively address the common failure points by replacing the valley cover gasket, fitting a new CPS, replacing the balance shaft assembly (if early), and rebuilding or replacing the Kompressor unit, giving the engine a fresh, reliable lease on life.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full M113 engine rebuild is highly justified for classic W220 S55 AMG Kompressor or W463 G55 AMG restorations where originality, matching numbers, and maximum longevity are required. An upgraded rebuild should include line-boring the block, new pistons/rings, and a balanced crankshaft.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Sourcing and fitting through our vetted network ensures your M113 engine is installed by specialists familiar with classic Mercedes V8 and Kompressor systems, backed by a nationwide warranty.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: Because the M113 is typically found in W210, W220, W463, and various AMG vehicles valued between £3,000 and £25,000+ (with low-mileage Kompressor models commanding significantly higher premiums), a full replacement is generally financially viable. However, if the lowest viable replacement cost exceeds approximately 60% of the vehicle's current market value, evaluate scrap value before committing .
